extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary criticism, poets and dramatists studying poetics and tragedy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging/constructing tragic poetry (Aristotelian poetics and its reception): what a tragedy must do, how plot and character should be built, and what aesthetic vs. moral standards apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blended pity-and-fear pleasure (cathartic effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The peculiar pleasure arising out of the union of the pitiable and the terrible” — tragedy should awaken in the mind the blended emotions of pity and fear which produce a pleasurable response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test of artistic merit in a tragedy is the degree in which it fulfils this distinctive function; Aristotle defines tragedy as effecting through pity and fear the proper catharsis (purgation) of these emotions. Examples/implication: the tragic plot and characters must be arranged to call forth this blend rather than mere sensationalism or sentimentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fulfilment of tragedy's distinctive function
rubrics_metrics.description: “The test of artistic merit in a tragedy is the degree in which it fulfils this, its distinctive function.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All technical rules Aristotle prescribes (plot construction, character, forms of recognition, etc.) flow from this primary requirement. If a play fails to produce the proper pleasure/catharsis it fails as tragedy even if it succeeds as moral instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper construction of the plot (unity, necessity, probability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot must be properly constructed—actions linked in a closely sequenced unity that works up to an inevitable end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle emphasises internal necessity and probability: events must follow from dramatic motive; gratuitous incidents or motiveless depravity that do not serve the plot are defects. The plot should be an integrated whole (serious, complete, of a certain magnitude) producing the tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of the ideal tragic hero (nobility/grandeur)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters portrayed in epic and tragic poetry should be σπουδαῖοι — morally noble or of heroic/‘elevated’ order (not merely ordinary virtue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle requires moral grandeur or elevation (not necessarily perfect virtue) so the character impresses the imagination and arouses grandeur-linked emotion. Defects may exist but should be of a kind that enhance tragic effect (e.g., hubris leading to reversal). The author warns against reducing goodness to prosaic common virtue; greatness must suit the magnitude of the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of vice only when necessary to plot
rubrics_metrics.description: “The representation of moral depravity finds its only excuse in 'necessity'… Gratuitous or motiveless depravity is forbidden.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immoral actions or depravity are allowable only when they are required by the inner necessity of the drama (they serve the proper play of contrasted character and lead to catastrophe). Example cited: Menelaus in Euripides’ Orestes as improper when gratuitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should depict the general, not the particular
rubrics_metrics.description: “Art ought to represent the general not the particular.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle condemns personal satire and treating single persons as the subject-matter of art; good art abstracts general human types/conditions rather than mere individual scandal. This is a ground for ranking personal satire as an inferior art form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic pleasure (delight) is the primary end of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: “Poetry is an emotional delight, its end is to give pleasure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle separates educational use from aesthetic enjoyment: for grown readers/listeners the chief end is refined, elevated pleasure. Moral instruction may occur but is secondary — 'poetry only instructs as it delights.' This contrasts with the older didactic view that poetry's primary office is moral teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge poetry by poetic standards, not external factual standards
rubrics_metrics.description: “The standard of correctness in poetry and politics is not the same… poetical truth and scientific truth are not identical.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical inaccuracies in medicine, natural science, or history do not vitiate poetic excellence so long as the work conforms to poetic laws (necessity, probability within its own assumptions). One should not test poetic representation by alien factual standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of presentation: enacted action, not narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should be 'in the form of action, not of narrative' — it is an enacted mimesis rather than merely told events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's definition stresses that the dramatic mode (drama as performance) is essential: action performed and organized in parts (with different rhetorical/artistic kinds found in separate parts) achieves the tragic effect more directly than narrative alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness, completeness, and magnitude of the action
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is 'an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The matter treated should be weighty and significant (not trivial), the action should stand as a whole (complete) and be of sufficient scale to warrant the elevated treatment and to produce the required emotions in the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate language and artistic ornament for separate parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy uses 'language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament, the several kinds being found in separate parts of the play.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different parts of the drama call for different modes/styles (chorus, lyrical passages, dialogue); language and ornament should be suited to the function of each part and contribute to unity and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid debased sentimentalism and mere sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism (e.g., Aristophanes' charge against Euripides) that substitutes 'the troubling of the senses for genuine tragic emotion' — using rags and stage-properties to provoke mere sympathy — is condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic pity must be genuine and arise from character and necessity, not from artificial properties or cheap appeals; sentimentality that substitutes sensory shock for true tragic pathos undermines the aesthetic end.
